content.comment_body: Hello, I'm attempting to activate the coils of a [product_name] 8.FS4 via Modbus TCP with Arduino. Initially, I tried using QModMaster, a Modbus simulation software, but it's not working as expected. After hours of searching, I realized I can't set the [product_name] Modbus TCP to Server mode—it only operates as a Client. From what I understand, to change coil states, a request must come from a client, with the server ([product_name]) responding. Any advice or assistance would be appreciated.

The [product_name] functions well as both client and server in Modbus TCP. To activate coils like Qx, Mx, and NQx, ensure these coil inputs aren't connected in your [product_name] program. For more details, searching for "Modbus" in forums—especially in German—can be helpful, as there are many examples. I can't assist with Arduino-specific communication, though. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks for your response. I've tested your shared program—it works for the [product_name] Q1 and M1. As a student, I can't get help at school, and tutorials for Modbus TCP on [product_name] are difficult to find. What needs to be set in [product_name] programming or configuration to modify coil states? I understand that when coils are in use on the left side, changes aren't possible. To enable or disable them, could I use a "VM" Holding Register alongside other activation conditions? How is this achieved? Additionally, I'd like to read an analog sensor from [product_name] (presumably through a "VM" Holding Register accessible at Modbus address 40001). With QModMaster, I can activate Q1 if I create a new Server Connection and add a "Q" (see the attached picture), then setting addresses 1, 2, or 3 and writing '1' activates the coil. I have the spreadsheet with your addresses, but I don’t fully understand it. Once I grasp the [product_name] side, I can handle the Arduino part. I’m open to compensating you for your assistance. Thank you!

Review the attached example for [product_name] as a Modbus server, with comments provided. Use your PC client to read inputs and write outputs. You'll need the correct IP for your [product_name] for the client setup. Selecting "Accept all connection requests" means [product_name] doesn’t need extra info, but you'll need to choose a client if multiple ones exist. Regards, [user_name]

Thank you! Things are nearly working, but there's one point I'm confused about. How was the amplifier assigned to VM100? I see that AI is Register 0 and AQ is Register 512, but I'm not sure how VM100 was defined. Thanks again.

This is a common issue lately—many try to find fast solutions without reviewing the operating instructions. Open "Tools" in [product_name] programming software and choose "Parameter VM mapping" to assign analog values to blocks. By selecting a block, you can set the parameter; type depends on the parameter, and the address can be freely chosen between 0 and 850. If a parameter shows a paper and pencil symbol, it means you can write it via Modbus. A good practice for address assignment is: Bit variables V0.0-V99.7, Byte variables VB100-VB199, Word variables VW200-VW398, Double word variables VD400-VD796. This prevents overlapping VM mapping for various value types. You can assign in any way, but following a system helps avoid confusion. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks for taking the time to help. I've spent three full days reading, which makes me feel a bit lost. I've worked for over a year with various controllers such as [version_no], Schneider, and Beckhoff, but I'm still struggling to work with [product_name] independently. Again, I appreciate your time.

I don't believe you're at fault, maybe just reviewing the wrong documentation sections. I've used [product_name] for years and sometimes forget my initial challenges, too. Wishing you success with Modbus and Arduino.
[user_name] Thank you! 👍 I recently started learning [product_name] 8. Your example helped me "connect" my Android with [product_name] [url] Best regards, [user_name]
